event_model_payload.summary:
Samartha Chandrashekar & Nick Parker

You click play on a Friday night, and in the second that follows, dozens of services answer in milliseconds. Most of them run on Titus, our internal container platform. Titus is, in essence, a Kubernetes-based container hosting platform: we keep both the control plane and the data plane (the container hosts that actually run containers) patched and up to date, so application teams get a consistent and reliable container experience. They hand us a container, and we run it, with no host, cluster, or kernel to own. Titus launches millions of containers every week across tens of thousands of EC2 instances in multiple AWS regions. It is multi-tenant by default: many containers from many teams share each host. That density is what makes container compute efficient, and it is why Titus has been the default home for so much of Netflix’s compute for years.

For most workloads, sharing a host works well. For a few, it does not, and those few include some of the most demanding real-time systems we run. This post is about them, and about single-tenant Titus, a mode that gives a task its own virtual machine while keeping everything else about Titus the same: the API, the deployment path, and the managed experience where the Compute/Platform team, not the application team, owns the host.

We will walk through why shared-kernel isolation runs out of road for certain workloads, how we measure isolation rather than asserting it, the options we weighed (microVMs, gVisor, EC2, and more shared-kernel tuning) and why a dedicated VM inside Titus won, how the mode is built on the Titus federation layer and autoscaling, and what we have seen along three axes: isolation, fleet efficiency, and the operational cost of keeping the fleet patched.

The cost of good neighbors

Multi-tenancy is a tradeoff. Packing many containers onto a large bare-metal instance keeps utilization high, but it also means those containers share a single Linux kernel and the underlying hardware. Titus isolates them with the tools the kernel provides: cgroups cap CPU, memory, and disk; namespaces give each container its own view of the system; seccomp and AppArmor restrict the system calls a container can make; the Completely Fair Scheduler divides CPU time; the iocost controller meters disk IO; and traffic shaping meters each container’s slice of the network. Each container also gets its own identity, IAM role, and security groups, so tenants are isolated for security and resource management.

These mechanisms provide isolation for what the kernel can partition. They cannot fully partition what is shared in hardware. A group of cores shares a last-level cache and a path to memory, so a container that suddenly pulls a lot of data from RAM evicts a neighbor’s cache lines and slows it down, even when both stay inside their CPU limits. There is no cgroup for memory bandwidth or cache residency, as there is for CPU shares. The interference is real, it is hardware, and it does not show up as either container exceeding its quota.

A noisy neighbor and a co-located app each stay within their cgroup CPU and memory limits, but both draw on a shared last-level cache and memory bandwidth that lack cgroup fences. The noisy neighbor takes most of it, so the co-located app stalls and its tail latency rises even though no one exceeded a quota.

We have written about this before. Predictive CPU isolation of containers at Netflix moved some placement decisions out of the kernel and into a service that forecasts each container’s CPU demand and re-pins containers to cores to reduce cache interference, formulated as a combinatorial optimization solved every minute. Noisy Neighbor Detection with eBPF instruments the kernel scheduler to surface per-container run-queue latency, so we can see a victim being starved in close to real time. And Mount Mayhem traced container-startup slowness to a global kernel lock amplified by modern CPU cache topology. Each of these raised the floor for everyone on the platform, and we are continuing that work.

A decade of shared-kernel isolation, at Netflix and across the industry, has not made co-tenancy invisible, because a noisy neighbor is not one problem but a family of them. Almost every physical resource a host shares is its own axis of interference, and a cgroup can fence very few of them:

  • CPU performance indeterminacy. Co-located threads contend for the run queue, so scheduling latency rises even while a container remains within its CPU quota. Separately, a neighbor with a large working set evicts a tenant’s last-level cache lines and saturates memory bandwidth, neither of which a CPU share can partition.
  • Network bandwidth and packets per second. Per-container shaping competes for link bandwidth, and receives processing runs in softirq context, charging one container’s packet work to whatever CPU a neighbor is running on. A flood of small packets exhausts a core’s softirq budget long before any bandwidth cap is reached.
  • Storage bandwidth and IOPS. A neighbor saturating a device’s queue serializes everyone’s I/O, and on cloud block storage, the per-volume and per-instance throughput ceilings are a shared budget in their own right.
  • Long tail. Page-cache reclaim, NUMA and cross-socket interconnect traffic, TLB-shootdown interrupts, PCIe and GPU contention, package-level power and thermal throttling, and contention on kernel global locks (the class of problem behind Mount Mayhem) each degrade neighbors in their own way.

What unites them is that they are physical, shared, and below the level a quota can reach. A platform can cap how much CPU time or memory a container is granted; it cannot hand each tenant its own slice of the memory bus, its own softirq budget, or its own portion of the last-level cache.

Of these, the network dimension has bitten hardest in our experience. Per-container bandwidth shaping uses a hierarchical token bucket (HTB) queueing discipline that serializes traffic with a global lock to account for each container’s bytes and packets. Under a flood of small packets from a single container, contention for that lock can burn kernel CPU and starve co-located containers of the time they need to process their own traffic, resulting in TCP retransmits and tail-latency spikes on services that did nothing wrong. The mechanism meant to prevent noisy neighbors becomes one.

The workloads most exposed to this are stateful, high-throughput streaming jobs: real-time data pipelines and stream processors that continuously move large volumes of data and maintain in-memory state. When one of these is perturbed, recovery is not cheap. A stream processor that falls behind or loses its place may have to restore from a checkpoint and pause processing for many minutes to catch up. For these jobs, intermittent interference from a neighbor is not a small slowdown that averages out; it is a stop-the-world event that pages an on-call engineer. The same teams report, accurately, that they never saw this on a plain EC2 instance.

Why we kept coming back to the VM

Full VM isolation, where a workload gets its own host and kernel, is the standard our customers are already happy with. The question was not whether VM isolation works; it was how to offer it without giving up what makes Titus worth using. We weighed four paths.

  1. Keep improving shared-kernel isolation. This helps every workload on the platform, needs no opt-in, and we are still investing in it (more on the roadmap below). Its limitation is structural. Each round of tuning narrows the gap without closing it, because the underlying hardware remains shared. Cache, memory bandwidth, and the kernel’s own shaping and scheduling locks are not things a container boundary can fully contain. Shared-kernel isolation is the right default and the wrong promise for a workload that cannot tolerate a bad minute.
  2. microVMs (Firecracker, Kata Containers). Lightweight VMs boot in about 150 milliseconds by emulating far less hardware than traditional VMs, which is why they power serverless platforms. They were the most appealing alternative on paper, and we carefully reviewed them. Three things made the cost hard to justify. First, the hardware virtualization they rely on is available only on bare-metal instances or through nested virtualization, and nested virtualization was not ready on the instance types we run at Netflix at the time, so adopting microVMs broadly would have constrained us to a narrow slice of the fleet. Second, there is no managed microVM service we could build on, which means we would have to run and maintain a virtualization layer ourselves: patching the hypervisor, live-migrating guests, and qualifying emulated devices. That is exactly the kind of operational surface we prefer not to own when we can avoid it. Third, even setting those aside, microVMs add virtualization overhead on CPU- and IO-bound work and do not support GPUs. Excellent isolation, but at a price in flexibility and operational load we were not willing to pay.
  3. gVisor. A user-space kernel that intercepts system calls provides sandbox-grade isolation without a hypervisor, thereby avoiding the bare-metal constraint. The catch is performance and dependency. Intercepting syscalls in user space adds overhead on IO-heavy paths, which are precisely the workloads we most need to protect, and the open-source project lags behind its internal counterpart in fixes and is effectively maintained by a single vendor. The isolation we would gain came with a throughput tax on the exact jobs we were trying to help.
  4. Move the workload to EC2. It is possible to run containers directly on EC2 instances. The problem is that the application team takes back the operational load that Titus exists to carry: choosing instance types, patching hosts, and sizing and scaling the fleet. For a team that came to Titus precisely to avoid those things, this is a regression in the experience, and the move between Titus and EC2 has historically been a one-way door that teams are reluctant to cross.

Spectrum of isolation options from lighter and more shared to stronger isolation: shared-kernel containers, then gVisor, then microVMs (Firecracker or Kata), then a full VM as used by single-tenant Titus, which is highlighted. Each option is annotated with its launch latency, overhead, and the entity that operates it; single-tenant Titus is a dedicated EC2 instance with no additional virtualization overhead.

There is also a question of what kind of isolation we actually need. microVMs and gVisor are built for security isolation between mutually distrusting tenants, the case where one tenant might actively try to attack or escape into another. Among Netflix teams, that threat model is more than the situation warrants. What these workloads need is resource and performance isolation: a guarantee that a neighbor cannot steal their CPU, cache, memory bandwidth, or network, not protection from a hostile co-tenant. A dedicated EC2 VM delivers exactly that, with hardware we do not have to emulate and a kernel we do not have to sandbox. We pay for the isolation we need rather than for a stronger security boundary.

microVMs and gVisor asked for a large, bespoke investment with real risk in order to approximate something we could get directly: a VM. Using EC2 to run containers provides the VM, but takes away the managed experience. So we took the direct route and brought single-tenant VM isolation into Titus itself, under the existing API and the existing shared-responsibility model.

How single-tenant Titus works

The idea is simple to state: a single-tenant task runs on its own EC2 instance, sized to fit it, with nothing else scheduled alongside. That instance is still a Titus container host that the Compute/Platform team owns and patches. The team running the workload sees the same Titus API and the same deployment path. Nothing about how they package or ship the job changes.

Side-by-side anatomy of a multi-tenant Titus, where multiple teams’ containers share one Linux kernel and the hardware beneath it and contend with one another, versus a single-tenant node where one task plus its platform sidecars owns the whole machine with no co-tenants.

Most of the work happens in the federation layer, the part of Titus that decides where a job runs (which cell, which capacity) before it is scheduled onto a node.

When a job is eligible for single tenancy, three things happen.

  1. Federation decides eligibility and the envelope. Eligibility is governed by an allowlist maintained by the Compute/Platform team; a team opts in by targeting a single-tenant workload group rather than flipping a flag in the public API. For an eligible task, federation tags it as single-tenant and records the set of instance families it may run on, ensuring consistent performance across the workload. Consolidating this decision in federation follows the same principle we use for routing in general: placement intelligence belongs in one place, above the individual cells, where it can account for capacity and availability across the region.
  2. Autoscaling provisions a dedicated node. Given a pending single-tenant task, our autoscaling implementation launches the smallest instance that satisfies the task’s requested CPU, memory, and GPU from the allowed families for the task just in time. Taking the tightest fit keeps the unused remainder of each dedicated node small. The next section covers this in detail.
  3. The scheduler enforces one task per node. Single-tenant pods are configured with pod anti-affinity to prevent colocation with other pods, along with a priority class that exempts the task from preemption. Single-tenant nodes are also tainted to prevent unrelated workloads from being placed there, with only single-tenant workloads tolerating this taint. We also disable defragmentation/repacking for these nodes, so a single-tenant task is never relocated to repack the fleet. Together, these mean a single-tenant task has its host to itself for its entire life, undisturbed by a neighbor or by the platform’s own bin-packing.

Two design choices are worth dwelling on. First, single tenancy is allowlisted on purpose. If it were a free checkbox in the API, most teams would tick it, because who wouldn’t want a quieter host? And the efficiency that multi-tenancy exists to provide would erode across the fleet. Keeping the Compute/Platform team in control lets us direct dedicated isolation to workloads that need it and steer the rest toward shared capacity, while keeping the public API surface small as we learn. Second, we do not silently resize anyone’s job to fill its node. The job keeps the resources it requested; we recommend sizing it close to a node shape so the dedicated instance is well utilized, while keeping the workload portable and running identically whether in single-tenant mode or not, regardless of the host’s dimensions. Moving in and out of the mode is a configuration change, not a rewrite.

A few perpetrators, a lot of collateral damage

Noisy-neighbor pain is not spread evenly. In practice, a small number of workloads cause most of the disruption: a job that floods the host with small packets, churns the page cache, or saturates memory bandwidth degrades the performance of every other container unlucky enough to share its host. Some of these are also among the workloads most affected by contention, because a job can be both a source of interference and sensitive to it. The shape of the problem is a few perpetrators and many victims.

That shape is what makes single tenancy a precise lever rather than a blunt one. We do not need to give every workload its own machine. We need to pull the handful of perpetrators and the most disruption-sensitive victims onto dedicated nodes. Doing so protects their former neighbors directly and removes the reason the platform was spreading sensitive workloads apart with anti-affinity placement in the first place. The hosts left behind are quieter, and because they no longer have to be kept partly empty to honor spread rules, they pack more densely.

Before-and-after view of the Titus fleet. Before: a few red perpetrators are scattered across shared hosts, the amber workloads beside them are disrupted, and anti-affinity spreading leaves dashed stranded capacity. After: each perpetrator runs on its own dedicated single-tenant node, the remaining shared hosts are fully loaded with healthy workloads, and one host’s worth of capacity is reclaimed.

On the left is the fleet before: perpetrators sit on shared hosts, the workloads next to them suffer, and anti-affinity rules leave gaps that cannot be filled. On the right is the same fleet after: each perpetrator has its own right-sized node where it can be as noisy as it likes, with no one to disturb; the remaining hosts run full of undisturbed workloads; and the capacity that used to be stranded comes back. A few dedicated nodes buy isolation for the perpetrators and a calmer, denser fleet for everyone else.

Provisioning many small nodes

Single tenancy trades fewer large, shared instances for more small, dedicated ones, and that shift has consequences across the stack.

The first is the control-plane load. More nodes mean more for the Titus control plane to track and more VM launches against the EC2 control plane, the latter mattering most during a regional failover, when we scale up the fastest and can least afford a throttle. Titus is already a federated system: each region is divided into independent cells, which limit how large any single control plane can get, and let us add capacity by adding cells rather than growing a single stack without limit. We migrate workloads in stages rather than all at once, and we exercise the launch-rate path under controlled load on a schedule rather than discovering its limits during an incident.

The second consequence is capacity management, where the design changed the most. With one task per node, the fleet now spans many instance shapes whose demand shifts continuously as jobs come and go. Pre-staging static pools of every shape would be slow to manage and wasteful, so we instead provision single-tenant nodes on demand. It handles provisioning end-to-end, and several of its features line up with exactly what single tenancy needs:

  • Just-in-time, right-sized provisioning. Single-tenant jobs are configured with a list of supported instance families based on their performance requirements. At launch, they are mapped to the best-fit node size by comparing requested resources against the selected instance families. New nodes of that instance type are brought up by the autoscaler to meet the pending demand. Single-tenant pods are configured with anti-affinity to all other pods, so the scheduler naturally lands one pod per autoscaled node. Newly vacated nodes may be reused by any pending deploys before they’re automatically torn down. The node pools themselves are shared across single-tenant workloads and describe a catalog of available instance families and sizes.
  • Single tenant node pools. Single tenant may run in separate clusters or be shared with multitenant clusters. The pools are configured with a list of supported instance-type permutations and are pinned to a Titus container host AMI. This is where the managed experience lives: the host image and its configuration are ours, declared once and applied to every node created.
  • Consolidation management. In multi-tenant environments, we default to a repack/defrag behavior that periodically relocates workloads. This doesn’t apply in single tenant, where nodes are explicitly each running at most one workload. We therefore reclaim only nodes vacated by workloads that have scaled in or terminated. Node termination is performed in two stages, allowing nodes to be reused for pending workloads before they are fully terminated.
  • Drift-based patching. When we publish a new container host AMI, we support a “mutable” deploy to existing nodes without affecting any hosted containers, and an “immutable” deploy that updates the target AMI for newly created nodes. This means that many node upgrades don’t require disrupting workloads, but we reserve the right to roll the fleet with our users if needed.

The launch-latency tax, and why warm pools are harder here

Provisioning on demand does not make a node appear instantly, and launch latency is the tradeoff single tenancy asks us to manage most carefully. Bringing a single-tenant task to the point where it can serve traffic has two parts: standing the node up (booting a fresh EC2 instance, then pulling and extracting the container image, which is the largest part of host setup for most jobs) and the application’s own startup (a JVM loading and JIT-compiling its classes, a cache filling, and so on). A fresh instance takes tens of seconds before the image pull even begins.

In multi-tenant Titus, most of this is hidden. A new task usually lands on a Titus container host that is already running and already has the image layers cached, so starting it takes only a few seconds rather than minutes; the host boot was paid for once, long ago, and amortized across every task that has run there since. Single tenancy gives up that hiding place. Every single-tenant task waits for its own machine to boot and pull its image.

The usual remedy is a warm pool: keep some instances booted and idle so a pending task lands on one immediately. This works well for the multi-tenant fleet precisely because that fleet is close to homogeneous. A handful of large shapes cover almost everything, since any task can be packed onto a big shared host. A small amount of warm capacity in a few shapes gives a high hit rate, and its cost is spread across the many tasks that will use it.

Single tenancy inverts those economics, and this is the part worth being explicit about.

Press enter or click to view image in full size

Because every task gets a right-sized node, the fleet spans many instance shapes (several families across many sizes), and a warm instance only helps a pending task whose shape matches it. A warm r7i.2xlarge does nothing for a task that needs an m7a.8xlarge. To achieve a good hit rate, we would need to hold idle capacity in every family-and-size bucket, and idle capacity in a bucket with no task to fill is pure cost. The very property that makes single tenancy efficient at steady state, tight best-fit sizing, works against warm-pool reuse: more distinct shapes mean more buckets and a lower hit rate per dollar of standing capacity. And the pressure peaks exactly when it is least welcome. During a regional failover or a live event, when many tasks need fresh nodes at once, a thin warm pool spread across many shapes drains immediately, and the rest of the demand pays the full cold-boot cost.

So we treat warm capacity as a small, targeted lever rather than a default. We keep a little pre-warmed capacity for the most latency-sensitive single-tenant starts, and we deliberately narrow the menu of shapes to a curated set of sizes rather than the full continuum, so warm capacity concentrates into fewer buckets and trades a little best-fit efficiency for a better hit rate. Everything else provisions just-in-time and accepts the boot.

The more durable wins are in cutting the launch cost itself rather than pre-paying for it, and they help both single- and multi-tenant nodes, which is the better place to spend the effort:

  • Faster image distribution. The image pull dominates the host setup, so newer OCI image formats and lazy-pulling snapshotters such as stargz and SOCI, which fetch only the bytes a container actually reads at startup rather than the whole image up front, reduce the largest component of the gap.
  • Checkpoint and restore. For processes that are slow to initialize, snapshotting a warmed-up application with a tool like CRIU and restoring it, rather than cold-starting it, removes most of the second half of launch latency.
  • Instance type selection. In multitenant configurations, we have historically used metal instances, which offer slightly better performance but come with a slower startup time. In a single-tenant configuration, node startup latency is more important, so we have moved away from these instances.
  • Scheduling optimization. Through regular stress testing of fleet scaling, we found a scheduling bottleneck caused by Kubernetes preemption logic, leading to nodes being scaled up quickly but then left idle while waiting for workloads to be scheduled on them. This was ultimately unnecessary, as our single-tenant pools do not run preemptible workloads. Disabling preemption greatly improved scheduling performance when under strain.

None of this makes the tradeoff disappear, and it is worth stating plainly: a single-tenant node is slower to stand up than a slot on an already-warm shared host, and hiding that with warm pools costs more per node here than it does on the multi-tenant fleet, because the warm pool cannot be as homogeneous. But for the long-running services that single tenancy targets, paying that cost once at launch in exchange for a quiet life afterward is a trade these teams are glad to make.

Measuring the difference

Isolation claims are easy to assert and hard to trust, so we measure them with a repeatable benchmark and a single score.

The method is a differential one. We run a reference container, a healthy and representative application, and record its throughput and tail latency while it runs alone. Then we run it again next to a havoc container engineered to be a bad neighbor: a UDP flood through XDP to stress the network-shaping path, pointer-chasing and STREAM to pollute the last-level cache and saturate memory bandwidth, fsync storms against the disk, stress-ng to abuse the scheduler, and GPU-burn to monopolize an accelerator. We only trust a run once the host has reached a steady state, which we confirm with the kernel’s Pressure Stall Information: we wait until cpu_some or mem_some shows that tasks are actually stalling on a contended resource, not merely that the resource is busy. Each scenario is run many times with fixed seeds, and we report the median with a bootstrapped confidence interval, because noisy-neighbor distributions are heavy-tailed and a simple average can mask the spikes that matter.

From the reference container’s numbers, we derive a simple measure of how well isolation held. Throughput efficiency is the fraction of operations per second the app retains under attack; latency efficiency is the ratio of its undisturbed P99 to its P99 under pressure. A neighbor that doubles the reference app’s P99 drops the latency efficiency. As an illustration, a reference app whose P99 latency goes down next to a havoc container achieves a certain latency efficiency, and one whose throughput falls from a to b operations per second achieves a certain throughput efficiency. The composite score is a weighted blend of the two, with a latency-sensitive preset that gives greater weight to tail latency for interactive and streaming-path services. A perfectly isolated system scores 100%, and a single hard failure invalidates the run regardless of the average.

Noisy-neighbor isolation

cgroups container isolation isn’t perfect, and applications may experience worse performance due to sharing a machine with a determined neighbor. This could extend to disk and/or network IO where the same volumes or interfaces may be shared across workloads. For a distributed workload, this can lead to measurable inconsistencies in performance depending on where the replicas are placed. For more sensitive workloads, this variance can mean the difference between stability and getting paged.

The single-tenant option makes it possible to better isolate workloads that cause problems for their neighbors and/or are more sensitive to such problems. This can be used as a stopgap until the specific regression problem is resolved and consistency is restored, or kept permanent for load patterns that aren’t worth supporting in a shared environment.

Efficiency

The second effect is fleet efficiency, and it is the one people expect to go the wrong way. Dedicating a node to a single task consumes that node’s slack, so the naive expectation is that utilization falls. In aggregate, it can move the other way, for a reason related to how we dealt with poor isolation before single tenancy existed.

To protect sensitive workloads on shared hosts, the platform used anti-affinity placement, scattering them across the fleet to reduce colocation of the same workload on the same nodes. Spreading fights bin-packing: it strains capacity, because a host kept partly empty to honor an anti-affinity rule cannot be filled by a workload that would otherwise have fit there. When isolation-sensitive workloads move to dedicated nodes, the need for spreading and fragmentation goes away, and the remaining multi-tenant fleet can pack more densely.

Another source of fragmentation is services that are sensitive to disruption. These are typically stateful services where recovery is expensive. As these services become more common in a given population, they can lead to nodes being held up by pods with strict disruption requirements. This can lead to an inability to defrag and recompact the pool during off-peak times. The symptoms and resulting drop in fleet efficiency caused by disruption-sensitive workloads mirror what’s observed for workloads with anti-affinity rules.

Depending on the magnitude of the anti-affinity and/or disruption budget problem, moving such workloads to single-tenant pools can result in equivalent or even improved placement when all costs have been accounted for. It also becomes easier to quantify the cost to end-users. Rather than trying to attribute fleet-wide fragmentation to individual workloads, we can directly quantify waste as single-tenant node overhead.

The theory and the practice diverge here, and it was the practice that decided it. In principle, the efficiency ceiling is higher for multi-tenant bin-packing: pack enough tasks together, and a host fills almost completely. We do not reach that ceiling. AWS offers a discrete set of instance sizes, so a large shared host rarely matches the exact sum of the requests we place on it, and the gap between a host’s capacity and what we can actually pack onto it is a bin-packing hole we cannot fill. At the granularity of large instances, those holes are sizable. Right-sizing an instance to a single workload, picking the closest fit from many shapes instead of draping many workloads over one big host, captured more of the available efficiency in our experience than the higher theoretical ceiling ever delivered. The clean theory favored multi-tenancy; our measured fleet favored right-sizing.

Container-host maintenance

The third effect is operational, and it shows up in how we keep the fleet patched. A multi-tenant host is hard to take down for maintenance precisely because it is full: draining it means relocating many tenants at once, several of which carry disruption budgets that limit how fast they can move, so a routine patch becomes a careful, coordinated evacuation. A single-tenant host runs exactly one task, with consolidation and defragmentation turned off, so draining it means relocating only the one workload, and we can automatically handle that when a new AMI ships. The remaining multi-tenant hosts are easier to maintain, too, because the workloads that were most sensitive to disruption are no longer stranded on them.

What it changes, and what it doesn’t

Single-tenant mode is a configuration, not a migration. A team moves a workload onto a dedicated node, and back, with a labeling change, without rewriting anything and without leaving Titus. That turns the isolation decision into a reversible setting, which is the opposite of the one-way door between Titus and EC2 that teams used to face. A team can try single tenancy for a quarter, measure it, and step back if the trade-off isn’t worth it for them.

What does not change is the contract. The Compute/Platform team still selects the instance type, patches the host, and sizes and scales the fleet underneath. The application team still uses the Titus API, the same delivery pipeline, and the same observability. Single tenancy is a new point on the isolation axis offered within the existing managed experience, not a separate product that the team has to learn and operate.

When a dedicated node is the wrong call

A dedicated node is a real cost, and single tenancy is not free isolation. Two things are worth weighing before reaching for it.

First, a single-tenant task does not get the whole machine; it gets the machine minus overhead. Every Titus container host, dedicated or shared, runs the platform sidecars, system services, the kubelet, and the host environment itself, and that overhead is a roughly fixed slice of CPU and a few gigabytes of memory. On a shared host, that slice is paid once and amortized across the many tasks running there. On a dedicated node, a single task handles it. Because the cost is fixed rather than proportional, it is punishing as a fraction of a small instance and negligible on a large one: a small dedicated node can lose tens of percent of its resources to overhead, while on the largest shapes it rounds to a couple of percent.

Second, because a task is placed on the smallest instance that fits it, there is usually a gap between what the task asked for and the next available shape, and on a dedicated node, that gap is pure waste, with no neighbors to soak it up. The two effects compound: fixed overhead plus the best-fit remainder set a ceiling on how much of a dedicated node a workload can actually use, and that ceiling is lowest exactly where people are tempted to reach for isolation casually, on small instances. However, this sizing waste can be reduced through coordination with the service owner as needed.

The guidance follows from the arithmetic. Single tenancy pays off for large, long-running, performance-sensitive, disruption-sensitive workloads, sized close to a node shape and run as fewer, larger replicas rather than many small ones. It is the wrong call for small, bursty, or highly elastic workloads, where the overhead fraction is high, the dedicated node sits mostly idle, and multi-tenant packing is both cheaper and faster to scale. This is also why the mode is allowlisted rather than a self-serve checkbox: the platform can keep workloads on the side of that line where they belong, and leave the ones that would gain little from a node of their own on the shared fleet, where they are cheaper to run.

Who’s using it

The first adopters are the workloads that motivated the work: real-time data infrastructure. Managed Apache Flink stream processing, streaming data connectors, and telemetry and logging pipelines were both the most frequent sources of network contention and the most damaged by it, because their recovery is expensive and their disruption budgets are tight. These are stateful, high-throughput jobs where a few seconds of starvation can cascade into minutes of catch-up, and where the platform’s own repacking used to be a source of disruption in its own right.

Moving them onto dedicated nodes removed the class of problem rather than mitigating it. The teams running them report stable operation, having previously seen intermittent, hard-to-attribute interference, and their jobs are no longer relocated by fleet repacking, removing a second, self-inflicted source of disruption. Latency-sensitive serving paths and a handful of GraphQL and edge services have followed for the same reason: a predictable tail matters more to them than a few points of bin-packing efficiency.

This is an ongoing rollout, not a finished one. We are widening the set of eligible workloads as we learn, using the largest production jobs as the stress test for the platform’s scaling assumptions, and watching the control-plane and EC2 launch-rate metrics as the count of small nodes grows. We have also been running periodic stress tests to exercise scaling ahead of real user workload, and making improvements to autoscaling and scheduling logic along the way.

What’s next

We are not done on either side of the tradeoff. On single tenancy, we are reducing launch latency with smarter pre-warming of common shapes, broadening the allowlist as scaling data holds up, and extending the model beyond long-running services as cost attribution and capacity stories mature. On the multi-tenant side, which remains the right default for most workloads, we are addressing the dimensions that hurt the most. The largest is the network: replacing HTB’s global-lock shaping with an eBPF-based Expected Departure Time approach that rate-limits by timestamping packets rather than contending on a lock, and pairing it with a lower-overhead container network device. We are also evaluating hardware cache and memory-bandwidth partitioning (Intel RDT and AMD PQoS) to give the kernel a real lever on the last-level cache, hardware GPU partitioning (NVIDIA MIG) for accelerator isolation, and continued work on the cgroup v2 IO controller for disk. This isolation benchmark lets us rank these by return on effort rather than by intuition, and show customers, in the numbers, that the shared fleet is getting quieter over time.

Single-tenant Titus is also a step toward something larger. Netflix’s Platform teams offer two ways to get compute: virtual machines on EC2 & containers on Titus. We want to replace that with a single Compute API that takes intent rather than mechanism into account: how much isolation a workload needs, how quickly it must launch, how long it can run without disruption, and what business domain it belongs to. The platform then makes placement and runtime choices, and can make globally optimal ones because it sees the whole picture.

Conclusion

Multi-tenancy is the right default for a container platform, and we will keep making it better for everyone. But the right default is not right for everything. Single-tenant Titus gives the workloads that need it the isolation of a dedicated VM, provisioned and patched by our existing node management, under the same API and the same managed experience, without taking away the freedom to change their mind. We can now point to the difference rather than describe it: a tail that stops moving under a noisy neighbor, a fleet that packs more densely once spreading is retired, and hosts that are faster and safer to patch. For the streaming and data systems at the heart of Netflix’s real-time platform, a room of one’s own turned out to be the feature that mattered.

Single-tenant Titus: VM-level isolation on a multi-tenant container platform was originally published in Netflix TechBlog on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

title: Ontology-Driven Observability: Building an End-to-End Knowledge Graph at Netflix Scale
summary:
Prasanna Vijayanathan, Renzo Sanchez-Silva

When Jake Paul and Mike Tyson stepped into the ring in November 2024, we delivered the fight to roughly 65 million concurrent streams. On an ordinary day our infrastructure takes in more than 2 billion requests and handles upwards of 38 million real-time logging events every second. At that scale, the whole picture doesn’t fit into a single engineering team’s head or onto a single dashboard. With more Live content, Podcasts and real-time streams, our need to understand and update our systems as quickly as possible becomes imperative to provide a good user experience. Understanding the system at this scale and within the time constraints we have, often becomes a daunting exercise in finding a needle in a haystack, in a dark jungle, blindfolded.

This post is about that search for the needle.

The Four hours before a fix

Consider a regression of the kind we see in a given week. The home screen where you see the list of lists of movies, starts taking about 1.5 seconds longer to render. An alert fires. And then we go looking for what caused this issue and how do we fix it?

As it so happens, a regression on the application could be related to anywhere in the system — a client app regression from a new version deployment or A/B test rollout, a load shedding in the infrastructure, a GraphQL query responding with bad data because of a service rollout 6 hops downstream, are all suspects at this point. So, answering “what caused the issue?” needs insights from across the system, and this involves combing through layers of data in a meticulous manner.

The MELT Layer

“What caused the issue?”

Metrics, events, logs and traces, or MELT, in the industry’s shorthand, are the right raw materials for such an investigation, and each of them answers roughly a quarter of the question. We collect observability data across these four pillars, unified into a single observability data layer. This lets us observe our systems in real time, across what our users are experiencing, how our applications are doing and what our backend infrastructure and services are processing and responding to.

title: Integrating Netflix’s Foundation Model into Personalization applications
summary:
Authors: Divya Gadde, Ko-Jen Hsiao, Dhaval Patel and Moumita Bhattacharya

The motivation for building the Netflix Foundation Model for personalization was laid out in this previous blog post. The Netflix homepage is powered by several specialized models and it requires significant time and resources to maintain and continue innovating on these individual models. Therefore, we decided to centralize member preference learning and have one powerful model learned from comprehensive user interaction histories and content data at a large scale and have this model distribute its learnings to other models.

Although the near-real time framework cannot be used for very large models, it represents an important direction for addressing embedding staleness and adaptiveness of recommendations.

This approach involves using the Foundation Model as an input to the downstream model i.e. the Foundation Model decoder stack is a subgraph of the application model’s full model graph and hence the name “subgraph integration”. The Foundation Model subgraph processes raw user interaction sequences and outputs representations that are then fed into the downstream model graph.

Applications can fine-tune the Foundation Model subgraph as part of their own training process, potentially leading to better performance than just using static embeddings. In this approach, there is no time gap or staleness between the Foundation Model inference and the application model’s inference, ensuring that the most up-to-date learnings are used. This approach also allows applications to leverage specific layers from the Foundation Model that may not be exposed through the Embedding Store, uncovering more application-specific value.

However, the subgraph approach comes with some complexities and trade-offs. To use the Foundation Model as a subgraph, application models need to generate all the features necessary for the subgraph as part of their feature generation process. This can add time, compute and complexity to their feature gen jobs. Merging the Foundation Model as a subgraph also increases the application model size and inference time. To alleviate some of these complexities, the Foundation Model team provides some reusable code and jobs that make the feature generation more compute efficient. To optimize the inference performance, we split the subgraph and ensure it only runs once per profile per request and is shared by all items in the request.

Overall, the subgraph approach allows for a deeper integration and enables the applications to harness the full power of the Foundation Model. But it can also make the application’s training code more complex, requiring a trade-off between metric improvement, compute cost, and time. Therefore, we would reserve this approach for high impact use cases where the increase in metric wins compensate for the cost and complexity.

This approach is similar to fine-tuning LLMs with domain specific data. In the previous blog post, we described how the Foundation Model is trained on a next-token prediction objective, with the tokens being different user interactions. Different interactions are of different importance to various surfaces on the Netflix website. For example, for the ‘Trending now’ row, recent interactions on trending titles might be more important than old interactions. Hence, the Foundation Model can be fine-tuned on more product specific data and then the fine-tuned model can be used to directly power the product. During fine-tuning, application teams can choose to do full parameter fine-tuning or freeze some layers. They can also choose to add a different output head with a different objective. We built a fine-tuning framework to make it easy for application teams to develop their own custom fine-tuned versions of the Foundation Model.

This approach offers the ability to adapt the Foundation Model to application’s specific data and objectives, making it optimized for their use case. A side benefit of this integration approach is that it provides a de facto baseline for new models/applications. Instead of coming up with a new model stack and spending months on feature engineering, new applications can directly utilize fine-tuned foundation models. However, this approach can lead to more models and pipelines to maintain across the organization.The latency and Service Level Agreements (SLAs) of the fine-tuned model must be carefully optimized for the specific application use case.

Conclusion

We are continuing to innovate on these integration approaches over time. For example, the Machine Learning Platform team is working on near-real time embedding inference capabilities to address the staleness issues with the embedding approach. We are also working on a smaller distilled version of the Foundation Model to reduce the inference latency of the subgraph approach. We also provide a fine-tuning framework to make it easy to fine-tune and leverage the Foundation Model. We also continue to refine and standardize the APIs used in these approaches to make it easy for application teams to use them. Overall, these three integration patterns provide a comprehensive framework for how Netflix applications can interact with and extract value from the Foundation Model.

title: DataJunction as Netflix’s answer to the missing piece of the modern data stack
summary:
by Olek Gorajek, Samuel Redai, Yian Shang

Intro

Our Netflix journey from data to dashboards, particularly within the space of the experimentation platform, always presented a unique set of challenges. This blog post aims to illuminate these hurdles and explain how an innovative open-source metric platform became instrumental in overcoming some of them. We’ll showcase the critical role that DataJunction played in streamlining our data workflows and enhancing our ability to derive meaningful insights from our vast datasets.

Metrics are the foundation of data-driven decision-making, but at many organizations, they are scattered, inconsistently defined, and difficult to discover or trust. At Netflix, this challenge first became apparent in our experimentation platform, where reliable metrics are essential for interpreting test results. But the complexity of the original tooling made it very difficult to understand and introspect these metrics both in terms of their definitions as well as their values.

Initial Problem

Scattered metric definitions, redundant datasets, and pipelines are often a natural effect of a fast-moving company with a large and powerful analytical workforce. This is a common problem in big data-driven firms, and it is not easy to solve across multiple departments, which are often governed by somewhat different rules and regulations. An easy-to-use, well-governed, and centralized semantic layer can help with these issues. Our initial problem was most evident in our Experimentation Platform team, where the previous system required:

  • extensive business knowledge
  • familiarity with experimentation conventions
  • and complex engineering practices

This led to metric authoring processes that would take weeks, which was a prohibitive requirement for Data Scientists and Analytics Engineers who wanted to onboard new metrics to the Experimentation Platform.

Enter DataJunction

To address this problem and to set ourselves on the path to a successful semantic layer solution in the future, we looked at several candidates. Among other solutions we evaluated Mando (an internal framework), Minerva (an open source semantic layer from AirBnB), and DataJunction (another open source solution, “DJ” for short). All of them had some strength, but DJ offered one thing that the others did not at the time: a solid SQL parsing and SQL generation engine. At the time of the POC, DJ was also the only open-source solution that stored all its definitions in a connected graph, similar to how relational databases store metadata on their views and queries. Easy “SQL wrangling” with rich metadata was the main feature that convinced us to try it for our immediate use case.

DataJunction originated from a similar internal Facebook project created (around 2015) by the data science and infrastructure (DSI) team, mainly as an answer to the need for metrics portability. During several iterations of the Deltoid project — which was the main experimentation platform at Facebook at the time — users were required to rebuild and repopulate their metrics when they wanted to move to the next version of Deltoid. But after implementing DJ and abstracting all metric definitions the team offered seamless migrations by separating the concerns between the metrics and the stats computation platform. That project was subsequently renamed to MDF (Metrics and Dimensions Factory) and promoted as a generic semantic layer used widely by various departments. In 2021, one of the Facebook engineers (Beto Dealmeida), started the DJ Github project and built out some basic functionality. Then together with some folks at Netflix expanded the scope further, and soon after that the project was introduced at Netflix. Following that introduction, three Netflix engineers (authors of this blog) together with a couple of external contributors, most notably Nick Ouellet, have been building out the remaining features of the platform.

Architecture Decisions

A critical design constraint for building DJ at Netflix was resource scarcity. We refused to compromise on product quality, choosing instead to limit the feature set. Although DJ was clearly capable of addressing many simultaneous problems across diverse use cases, our lack of adequate resources and official support meant we developed it as a side project for over two years. Our hope was that demonstrating its value would eventually secure management attention.

API First, UI and Other Interfaces Later

A metrics platform doesn’t need a flashy front-end to deliver value — its core is the semantic layer, which stores a consistent set of dimensions and metrics and serves this information through a rich API service. You can see below how we structured the main components of DataJunction in the Netflix implementation. Our DJ services (in the middle) interact with the underlying data (on the left) and supply our access layer with the business definitions in the form of SQL w/ metadata or directly with data depending on the client request.

Consistent Graph First, Other Features Later

A complete semantic layer system can seem like an octopus, with its tentacles reaching out into many functional areas and can expand from a basic semantic metadata stored for some datasets to full dashboard functionality. Let’s call out some of them:

  • semantic metadata authoring and management and monitoring
  • metric and dimension query / definition generation
  • metric and dimension data generation (requires a query engine)
  • data visualization and data tracking
  • performance optimization (aka caching or materialization)
  • integration layer with other tools and
  • any / all the above functionality served as: UI, API, client libraries, MCP servers and more.

Of course it is extremely hard to provide the best in class functionality across all these layers, so with our small “unofficial” team we decided to focus on the most important piece: solid semantic layer engine (and API) with the ability to parse SQL as the input to the graph and generate SQL as the serving layer. That is the core of the system and everything else can be added later with less effort and w/o the need to rebuild the core.

Cube as The Perfect Consumption Protocol

Analytical multi-dimensional cubes have been a fundamental concept for decades, with their representation integrated across various data processing and analysis platforms. While definitions and features may vary between tools, they all serve the common purpose of encapsulating, or abstracting, a subset of semantic objects.

In DataJunction, we adopted cubes as first-class features for two main reasons: their familiarity to users and their suitability as a serving interface. They efficiently deliver both the semantic definitions (of metrics and dimensions) and fast data access. See an example of data “flow” graph (dotted lines) and dimensional relationships graph (solid lines) below.

We simplified the creation of basic cubes, allowing them to easily aggregate arbitrary collections of shared metrics and dimensions. Furthermore, accessing, managing, and visualizing these cubes is straightforward for any client integrating with DJ. Custom integrations, such as for Netflix’s internal fast Druid data analysis tool (Data Explorer → see below), became trivial to build, and we also made it easy to materialize these cubes directly in our Druid clusters.

One of DJ’s most powerful client integrations is the ability to link any DJ-originating metric definition back to the DJ ecosystem. This creates a valuable feedback loop: troubleshooting and introspecting business dashboards becomes simple if they display DJ-defined metrics that include links back to the definition source. This link then makes inspecting and running ad-hoc analysis, by modifying existing metrics, a trivial process. This integration is not only possible with our inhouse tools, but also with other well known open-source products, like Superset.

Experimentation at Netflix

Metrics are the backbone of experimentation. They translate data into signals that tell us whether a change is meaningful, safe, and worth scaling. Without trustworthy metrics and dimensions, experiments risk becoming inconclusive or misleading, so a robust metrics layer becomes crucial for data-driven decisions.

At Netflix, the original metrics layer integrated into the experimentation platform was overly complicated. Creating new metrics not only required tribal knowledge of experimentation data artifacts, but also familiarity with complex engineering workflows. This unnecessary friction meant that onboarding a single new metric could take weeks, slowing adoption of new metrics and hindering experimentation.

This is where DataJunction comes in: it provides a central hub for defining metrics and dimensions that can easily be shared and explored via the semantic graph. It also provides flexible, user-friendly interfaces (including a UI, API, and various clients), making it easy for users to author and manage their metrics and other semantic models.

Conclusions

With experimentation domain well supported by DataJunction, we would like to take on next steps to unifying of the general analytics at Netflix and to make it easier for Netflix users to both:

  • find and use metric definitions across verticals (defined in DJ)
  • easily access, modify and experiment with new metrics across Netflix data stack

That will require building out strong integrations between DJ and other tools, but that has been underway and it is one of the most enjoyable parts of this project, where most of the feature exists and we are simply enabling existing systems to exchange information in a structured and reliable way. With a system like DataJunction our internal LLMs can deliver accountable information about the business metrics as well as explanation of how they are defined and used across Netflix.

Related resources:

  • 2023 : DataJunction at Netflix (slide deck)
  • 2025 : DataJunction talk at Data Engineering Open Forum 2025 (video)
  • 2025 : DataJunction: Unifying Experimentation and Analytics (blog)

title: Measuring the Impact of Personalized Recommendations
summary:
By Kevin Zielnicki, Guy Aridor, Aurélien Bibaut, Allen Tran, Winston Chou, and Nathan Kallus

Introduction

Personalization is everywhere on the internet. It shapes the products we discover, the stories we read, the music we hear, and the movies and TV shows we watch. At Netflix, personalization has been central to the member experience for decades — from the Netflix Prize to our modern recommender system that helps members navigate a large and constantly changing catalog.

But personalization is not only an algorithmic problem, it is also a measurement problem. How do we know how much value personalization creates? More precisely, how do we separate the appeal of a title from the value created by recommending that title to the right member at the right time?

In a new article in the International Journal of Industrial Organization — which we are also presenting at this year’s ACM Conference on Economics & Computation (EC ‘26) — we develop a model of member behavior, title choice, and personalized recommendations. The model lets us estimate how recommendations affect both whether members choose to watch and, if so, which titles they choose. In this post, we summarize our approach and main findings.

The Measurement Challenge

A natural first attempt at valuing recommendations is to ask: what share of viewing comes from titles that were recommended? This is an intuitive metric, but it fails to answer the causal question at hand.

The problem is that recommendations are not randomly assigned. A title appears on a member’s homepage precisely because the recommender system predicts that the member might want to watch it. If a member watches that title, was it because the recommendation caused the member to watch it? Or would she have watched it anyway because of her underlying preference for that kind of title? This is the core measurement challenge: recommendations are targeted to demand, so viewing a recommended title combines the effect of personalization with the member’s underlying preferences.

One way to solve this would be to run a large experiment that replaces Netflix’s personalized experience with an unpersonalized one. That would create clean variation — but it would also be a poor member experience. Personalization is a central part of how members locate valuable titles in a large catalog, so turning it off broadly is not an acceptable measurement strategy.

Instead, we take a hybrid approach. We build a behavioral model that separates members’ underlying preferences from the incremental effect of recommendations. The model uses the natural variation in the recommendation system, for example due to algorithmic exploration, to estimate how recommendations affect choice. Then, to validate the model predictions about title substitutability, we use small-scale A/B tests that “nudge” the salience of a handful of titles exogenously, generating ground-truth substitution patterns for a subset of titles. This lets us combine the scale and richness of modeling with the credibility of experimental evidence.

A Model of Member Choice

To measure the value of personalization, we need a model of what members would watch under different recommendation systems. Our model treats Netflix viewing as a day-by-day choice process. On each day, a member chooses among the titles available in the catalog, or she chooses not to watch anything. This gives us a concrete target to estimate: the probability that a member watches each title on a given day, as a function of their preferences, their viewing history, and the recommendations they see.

A simple version of this model would be too restrictive. It might assume, for example, that removing one title from the catalog shifts viewing toward all other titles in roughly proportional ways. But that isn’t how member choice works. If a member is considering a romantic comedy, the closest substitutes are likely other romantic comedies, not every title on Netflix equally. For similar reasons, two members may react very differently to the same recommendation.

To capture this complexity, we use a low-rank choice model. The model learns a representation of each title and a corresponding representation of each member’s current preferences. These representations are not limited to manually specified features like genre, cast, or language. Instead, they are learned from viewing behavior itself, allowing the model to capture nuanced similarities between titles that may be difficult to describe with coarse features, such as genre or release date, alone.

Member preferences are dynamic. What someone wants to watch today depends on what they have watched recently. A member who just finished a crime thriller may be in a different preference state than the same member after watching a stand-up special or a kids’ movie. Rather than estimate a fixed preference vector for each member, the model summarizes each member’s past viewing history into a current preference state. This lets us capture heterogeneous and time-varying tastes while also scaling to millions of members.

The key component for our purposes is that the model explicitly parameterizes the effect of recommendations. When a title is recommended, the model gives it an additional recommendation effect, or “bonus,” that increases its probability of being chosen. This bonus is a reduced-form way to capture two related mechanisms. First, recommendations can create awareness by helping members discover titles they may not have known about. Second, recommendations can provide information by signaling that a title is likely to be a good match.

Once estimated, the model becomes an engine for predicting counterfactuals. We can ask what would happen if a title were not recommended, if a different set of titles were recommended, or if the current recommender system were replaced with simpler alternatives. Because the model separately represents member preferences, title appeal, and recommendation effects, it lets us estimate not only how recommendations affect total viewing, but also how they change which titles are watched.

The model is only useful, however, if it captures real substitution patterns. The next step is therefore validation: comparing the model’s predictions to randomized experiments that directly perturb, on a small scale, the visibility that each title receives.

Validating the Model with Randomized Experiments

The model relies on an important assumption. After conditioning on the member, title, and state information available to the recommender system, we treat the remaining variation in whether a title is recommended as if it were randomly assigned. In our setting, this assumption is reasonable: we observe all of the information available to the recommender system, so we should be able to model its behavior accurately. But it is still an assumption. A useful model should not only fit historical viewing patterns; it should also predict what happens when recommendations change for external reasons.

Thus, to validate the model, we used randomized experiments that introduce variation in title visibility exogenously. These experiments mirror the kinds of variation that occur routinely when recommendation algorithms are updated: some titles receive more impressions, while others receive fewer. The key difference is that, in the validation experiment, this variation was prespecified so that we could estimate clean experimental benchmarks.

Specifically, we randomly assigned members to treatment arms that slightly nudged recommendations towards and away from different categories of titles. This let us measure diversion ratios: when a set of titles becomes less visible, how much viewing shifts to other titles, and how much shifts out of Netflix viewing altogether?

We then asked whether the model could reproduce those experimentally measured substitution patterns. We estimated the model on the control group, simulated the same recommendation changes, and compared the model-implied diversion ratios to the experimental ones. The agreement was strong: the model’s predicted diversion ratios had a correlation of 0.86 with the experimental estimates and an R-squared of 0.73.

This validation gives us confidence that the model captures counterfactual substitution patterns accurately. Subsequently, we ask what would happen under more dramatic changes, such as different recommender systems.

Counterfactuals: Aggregate Consumption and Diversity

With a validated model in hand, we can move from measurement to counterfactuals. Instead of asking only what happened under the current Netflix experience, we can ask what would have happened if members had seen recommendations generated by a different system.

We compare the current recommender system to three baselines:

  1. The first is random recommendations: every member receives titles selected uniformly at random from the catalog. This is not intended as a realistic product experience, but it helps isolate the value of having recommendations that are relevant.
  2. The second is popularity-based recommendations: every member receives broadly popular titles. This is a natural non-personalized benchmark.
  3. The third is a basic matrix factorization model, a classic personalized recommendation approach and a useful baseline for older generations of recommender systems.

In each counterfactual, we replace the recommended titles while keeping the rest of the choice environment fixed. This lets us estimate how much viewing would change if the recommendation policy changed, holding constant the catalog, members, and model of member choice.

The results show that the current recommender system generates substantially more engagement than each benchmark. Relative to the current system, random recommendations reduce engagement by 16%, popularity-based recommendations reduce engagement by 12%, and matrix factorization reduces engagement by 4%. These are large differences at Netflix scale. Even the comparison to matrix factorization — a personalized baseline — suggests that continued improvements in personalization translate into meaningful gains in how effectively members find titles they want to watch.

Engagement is only part of the story. A recommender system could increase viewing while concentrating attention on a narrow set of already-popular titles. That would be a worse experience for members whose tastes are not well represented by those titles, and it would make poorer use of a broad catalog.

We therefore also examine consumption diversity: how broadly viewing is distributed across titles. The current system performs well on this dimension too. Popularity-based and matrix-factorization recommendations both substantially increase concentration, meaning that fewer titles receive meaningful viewership. Random recommendations produce slightly more diversity, as expected, but at a large cost to engagement.

Taken together, these counterfactuals show that the value of personalization is not just that members watch more. It is also that members are matched to a broader set of titles. The current recommender system increases engagement while preserving a wide distribution of viewing, reflecting the diversity of member tastes across the Netflix catalog.

Decomposing the Impact on Titles

The aggregate counterfactuals show that personalization increases engagement while maintaining broad consumption across the catalog. We can also use the model to ask a more granular question: why does a recommended title get watched?

There are three conceptually distinct channels:

  1. The first is exposure: simply showing a title to a member can increase the probability that the member watches it. This captures the basic value of surfacing a title that may otherwise have been hard to find.
  2. The second is selection: recommended titles are shown to members who already have a relatively high baseline probability of watching them. This channel doesn’t lead to incremental engagement, but it can smooth the discovery experience and help users feel that the recommender system understands their preferences.
  3. The third is targeting: the recommender system may identify members for whom the recommendation itself is especially effective, meaning members who are much more likely to watch the title when it is recommended than when it is not.

The distinction matters because not all recommendation-driven viewing should be interpreted the same way. If recommendations worked only through exposure, then any reasonably visible surface could generate much of the same value. If they worked mostly through selection, then recommendations would mainly be finding members who were already likely to watch a title. Targeting is different: it captures whether the system is placing titles in front of members for whom the recommendation changes the decision.

Our model lets us estimate these channels title by title. For each title, we can compare the predicted probability that a targeted member watches it when recommended to the probability that an average member watches it when not recommended. We then decompose that difference into selection, exposure, and targeting.

We first show that exposure is meaningful: showing a title to an average member roughly triples its consumption probability relative to the baseline. Exposure is not the main driver of differences in consumption, as mechanical exposure explains only about 7% of the gap under the current recommender system, while selection and targeting account for the vast majority of the difference and the targeting effect is nearly seven times larger than the exposure effect.

This pattern is especially informative when compared with simpler recommendation systems. Random recommendations are dominated by exposure because they do not personalize: differences in consumption mostly reflect differences in what titles are shown. Matrix factorization changes this by making recommendations personal, reducing the role of exposure and leaving exposure, selection, and targeting to contribute nearly evenly to consumption differences. The current recommender system goes further: its gains come less from mechanical exposure, but more from targeting the right titles to the right viewers.

Targeting is also not uniform across the catalog. It is strongest for mid-popularity titles: titles with enough potential audience to be broadly relevant, but not so much mass appeal that everyone already knows about them. Very popular titles need less help from targeting, while very niche titles may have too small an audience to target effectively. The largest gains come from the middle of the catalog, where personalization helps connect specific titles with specific member tastes.

Conclusion

Personalized recommendations are valuable because they help members navigate a large catalog and find titles they want to watch. They are also valuable to Netflix because they make the service more useful, more engaging, and better able to serve a wide range of tastes.

But measuring that value is not straightforward. Recommendations are targeted by design, so we cannot simply compare recommended and non-recommended viewing. At the same time, turning off personalization at scale would create a worse member experience.

Our approach combines a large-scale model of member choice with true experimental validation. The model lets us separate underlying title preferences from the incremental effect of recommendations, and the experiments verify that the model captures real substitution patterns.

Using this framework, we find that personalization affects both how much members watch and which titles they watch. The value of recommendations comes not just from exposure, but from matching the right titles to the right members.

title: TimeSeries Tiered Storage Journey: Kafka/Flink Streams to Native Cassandra Cold Reads
summary:
By Oleksii Tkachuk, Rajiv Shringi, Chris Lohfink, Abe Ratnofsky, Kartik Sathyanarayanan

Introduction

In an earlier post, we introduced the TimeSeries Abstraction, our high-throughput, low-latency platform designed to store and query temporal event data at scale. It has since become the operational backbone for Netflix’s largest datasets, which now span multiple petabytes.

However, managing such large datasets in hot storage, tuned for low-millisecond latency access, is not cheap. At Netflix, cost-efficiency is a continuous discipline rather than a temporary initiative. This post shares two solutions that significantly reduce storage costs by continuously moving older, less frequently accessed data into cheaper object storage:

  • Solution 1: Uses Apache Kafka and Flink to stream data directly to S3
  • Solution 2: Leverages Cassandra backups in S3 and pluggable Memtables to read data directly from S3

We’ll start with the Kafka/Flink-based design, then describe how we evolved to a native Cassandra-based cold tier.

Challenges

As Netflix’s TimeSeries datasets have expanded, we’ve encountered several compounding challenges:

  • Growing retention demands: Users often push for increasing data retention to serve a broader range of use cases, which in turn increases the storage costs.
  • Escalating costs: Maintaining massive, dense clusters for infrequently accessed historical data is prohibitively expensive.
  • Sparse historical access: Most queries target recent events, but older data must remain readily available for occasional audits and investigations.
  • Operational strain: High storage density on hot nodes complicates scaling, deployment, and cluster stability.
  • Latency requirements: Even historical data sometimes requires sub-second query performance for internal tooling and analysis.

This creates a clear opportunity: keep the most recent data on fast storage and migrate older, rarely read data to cheaper storage while preserving a consistent API. Done well, this can meet user and operational needs while greatly reducing our infrastructure spend.

TimeSeries Abstraction

Before we dive into the cold storage solutions, here is a quick recap of how TimeSeries partitions its dataset into multiple tables, each covering a window of time we call Time Slices.

This enables several key optimizations, most notably allowing a table to become immutable once it crosses the write boundary, which lets us safely apply further optimizations. For more details, refer to our previous post.

This slice information is critical and is maintained in a dedicated metadata table:

Creating new Time Slices and maintaining their metadata is a primary responsibility of the TimeSeries control plane. The TimeSeries data plane uses this information to correctly route the read and write traffic to the provisioned tables.

With that background, let’s look at the different solutions we built for data tiering.

Solution 1: Streaming with Apache Kafka and Flink

Our first solution followed a familiar streaming pattern using Apache Kafka and Flink, where we streamed data to S3 in realtime while simultaneously persisting it to Cassandra.

Getting Data Into S3 Efficiently

To optimize data streaming to S3, the system hash-partitions Time Series IDs into buckets. This partitions the stream and lets dedicated Flink tasks handle each bucket, ultimately batching and reducing the write throughput to S3. Flink workers batch events into Parquet files grouped by event time within the hour. These files are great for high-throughput streaming writes, but not for low-latency reads.

Enter the Compaction job.

Compaction Job to Optimize Reads

The compaction job runs daily and merges small Parquet files into a single, optimized daily Parquet file per namespace.

The job further optimizes the Parquet files in the following ways:

  • Small Row Groups: Creates small (4–8 MB) row groups to minimize lookup cost. We can then use the Parquet Java library to perform range reads of row groups from S3. This is intentionally well below Parquet’s recommended row group floor — smaller groups were better because our reads are dominated by point/range lookups rather than full scans.
  • Event Sorting: Sorts events within a row group by time, eliminating brute-force scans when querying for a time range.
  • Bloom Filters: Caches Bloom filters and file metadata in EVCache, allowing the TimeSeries query planner to efficiently skip unnecessary reads from S3.

Once the compaction job completes, all compacted files per partition are recorded in the TimeSeries control plane, and the hot storage slices can now be truncated!

On some of our largest datasets, this job typically takes about 12 hours, prioritizing lower compute costs over execution speed.

Streaming Cold Tier Read

Once compacted files are optimized in cold storage, they are ready to be read. The TimeSeries data plane fans out a given query across both the hot and cold tiers and merges their result. The users still use the same query interface:

The Cold Tier Data Plane uses compaction metadata for aggressive planning and pruning, which dramatically reduces the S3 query fan-out. As a result, retrieving a full day of data requires at most three sequential S3 reads, even in the uncommon case where an ID spans two row groups. This yields a p50 latency of ~150 ms and a p99 latency of ~500 ms per read.

Why not stop here?
